summary.text: A 60-year-old female presented to the emergency department with right knee pain after a mechanical fall, one month after a right total knee arthroplasty with an unremarkable postoperative course. She had mild swelling, full passive range of motion and could bear weight with assistance. Radiographs showed intact prosthetic components without fracture, loosening or malalignment, and she was discharged with conservative management.

At a subsequent outpatient orthopedic clinic visit she reported persistent anterior knee pain and subjective weakness with ambulation, and examination revealed extensor mechanism insufficiency. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a complete rupture of the patellar tendon, which was definitively confirmed during surgical exploration. She was counseled on treatment options, including reconstruction with an Achilles tendon allograft, and chose to proceed with surgery.

Reconstruction used an Achilles tendon allograft with a bone block secured in a tibial trough by a screw, with the tendon branches fixed to the patella, quadriceps tendon and retinacula, and the native tendon stump incorporated. Patellar height and continuity were confirmed intraoperatively and there were no complications. Postoperatively she used an immobilizer, stayed non-weight bearing, and at the clinic visit had improved knee stability and restored active extension without infection, graft failure or wound complications.
